title: Post Office Protocol - Version 3
subtitle: How a mail client fetches its messages from a server and then lets the server forget them.
summary: POP3 lets a workstation that is not always online, or that cannot run a mail server, collect the mail waiting for it in a maildrop on a server. The client opens a TCP connection to port 110, logs in, lists and downloads messages, marks them deleted, and quits, at which point the server really removes them. It is deliberately simple: the intelligence lives in the client, not the server.

eli5.summary: Your mail sits in a mailbox at the post office. POP3 is you walking in, showing your ID, picking up your letters, telling the clerk which ones you no longer need, and leaving.

questions: what is the difference between pop3 and imap
what does the apop command do
when does pop3 delete messages from the server

tldr.problem: Small or intermittently connected machines cannot run a mail server, yet their users still need to read mail.
tldr.mechanism: A server holds each user's mail in a maildrop, and the client connects over TCP port 110 to log in, list, retrieve and delete messages in a short session.
tldr.outcome: It is a simple, widely implemented way to download mail, but it sends passwords and mail in the clear unless wrapped in TLS, and it offers little server-side mail management compared with IMAP.

lineage.title: How mail is sent and fetched

today: POP3 is still widely offered by mail providers and widely supported by mail clients, though IMAP is the usual choice for people who read mail on several devices. Today it is normally run inside TLS: RFC 2595 describes using TLS with POP3, and RFC 8314 recommends TLS for mail access and treats cleartext as obsolete. The command set in this RFC is still the core of what clients and servers speak.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Some machines in the Internet are too small to be a mail server. A workstation may lack the cycles and disk to keep an SMTP server (RFC 821) and a local delivery system running all day, and a personal computer may be connected to the network only now and then. Yet their users still want to read and manage mail through a user agent.

The RFC's answer is to let a machine that can run a message transport system offer a maildrop service. The Post Office Protocol, version 3 (POP3) lets a workstation "dynamically access a maildrop on a server host in a useful fashion", usually to retrieve the mail the server is holding for it. The RFC names the two sides the client host and the server host.

POP3 is not meant for rich mail management on the server. The RFC says that "normally, mail is downloaded and then deleted", and points to IMAP4 (RFC 1730) as the more advanced and complex alternative.
sections.eli5: Some computers are like a kid's lemonade stand: too small to run a whole post office. So a bigger computer keeps their mail safe, and POP3 is how the little one comes by to pick it up.

sections.title: A short digression: sending mail
sections.content:
POP3 only covers receiving. The RFC says it does not specify how a client enters outgoing mail into the transport system, but it offers a method "consistent with the philosophy of this memo".

When the user agent on a client host wants to send a message, it opens an SMTP connection to its relay host and gives it all outgoing mail. That relay host could be the POP3 server host, but it does not have to be. It must accept mail for delivery to arbitrary recipient addresses, which the RFC notes is not required of all SMTP servers.

So a typical mail client talks two protocols: SMTP to push mail out, and POP3 to pull mail in. They are independent, and neither knows about the other.
sections.eli5: Picking up letters and posting letters are two different jobs. POP3 is only for picking up. Posting is done with a different protocol, SMTP.

sections.title: Basic operation
sections.content:
The server listens on TCP port 110. A client connects, the server sends a greeting, and they then exchange commands and responses until the connection closes.

A command is a case-insensitive keyword of three or four characters, optionally followed by arguments of up to 40 characters each, separated by single spaces and ended by CRLF. A response starts with a status indicator, +OK or -ERR, which servers MUST send in upper case, and is at most 512 characters long including the CRLF.

Some responses are multi-line. After the first line, the server sends more lines and ends with a line holding only a period (CRLF.CRLF ends the response). A data line that itself starts with a period has an extra period put in front of it. The RFC calls this byte-stuffing, and the client strips it off.

A server MUST answer unknown, unimplemented, syntactically invalid or wrong-state commands with a negative status. The client cannot tell "not implemented" from "unwilling".

The session moves through three states, shown below. An optional inactivity timer, if used, must be at least 10 minutes. If it fires, the server closes the connection without deleting anything.
sections.eli5: The client and server talk in short lines. The server always starts with "OK" for yes or "ERR" for no. A long answer ends with a single dot on a line by itself, like a full stop at the end of a story.

sections.title: The AUTHORIZATION state
sections.content:
After the TCP connection opens, the server sends a one-line positive greeting such as +OK POP3 server ready. The session is now in the AUTHORIZATION state, and the client must identify itself. This RFC describes two ways: the USER and PASS pair, and APOP. Extra mechanisms are in RFC 1734. No single method is required, but a server must support at least one.

With USER name the client names a mailbox, the server answers +OK, and then PASS string supplies the password, which the RFC says is sent "in the clear on the network". With APOP name digest the greeting carries a timestamp such as <1896.697170952@dbc.mtview.ca.us> that must differ on every greeting. The client computes the MD5 digest (RFC 1321) of the timestamp followed by a shared secret and sends it as 32 lower-case hexadecimal characters (16 octets).

On success, the server takes an exclusive-access lock on the maildrop, numbers the messages from 1, notes each size in octets, and moves to TRANSACTION. If it cannot lock or open the maildrop it answers -ERR, and the client can try again or send QUIT.
sections.eli5: First you have to prove who you are. You can say your name and a secret word, or you can mix the secret word with a one-time number the server gave you and show only the result, so nobody who is listening learns the word.

sections.title: The TRANSACTION state
sections.content:
Once the maildrop is locked and open, the client can issue these commands as often as it likes. Each message is referred to by its number in the maildrop.

STAT
Returns +OK nn mm: the number of messages and the maildrop size in octets, not counting messages marked deleted.
LIST [msg]
A scan listing: message number and exact size in octets. With no argument it is multi-line and covers every message; with one it covers just that message.
RETR msg
Sends the whole message as a multi-line response, byte-stuffed.
DELE msg
Marks the message as deleted. It is not really removed until the UPDATE state.
NOOP
Does nothing and returns +OK.
RSET
Unmarks any messages marked as deleted.

A message marked deleted cannot be named again. Referring to it gets an error, and it vanishes from STAT and LIST. The RFC strongly discourages adding extra information to drop and scan listings, preferring optional commands that let the client parse messages itself.
sections.eli5: Now you are inside the post office. You can ask how many letters you have, ask how big each one is, take one, put a sticky note on one that you want thrown away, or peel all the notes off again.

sections.title: The UPDATE state
sections.content:
When the client sends QUIT from the TRANSACTION state, the session enters the UPDATE state. The server permanently removes every message marked as deleted, releases the lock on the maildrop, says goodbye, and closes the TCP connection.

If something goes wrong during removal, such as a resource shortage, the response is -ERR some deleted messages not removed. In that case some or none of the marked messages may have been removed, but "in no case may the server remove any messages not marked as deleted".

Deletion only happens after a clean QUIT. If the connection drops, the client times out, or QUIT is sent from the AUTHORIZATION state, the session does not enter UPDATE and the server MUST NOT remove any messages. This protects the user from losing mail the client never finished downloading.
sections.eli5: The sticky notes only count when you say goodbye properly. If you run out of the door in the middle, nothing gets thrown away.

sections.title: Optional commands and operations
sections.content:
Beyond the minimal set, the RFC defines optional commands, which it "strongly encourages" implementers to support instead of inventing richer listings. TOP msg n returns the headers, the blank line, and the first n lines of the body, so a client can preview mail without fetching it whole. UIDL [msg] returns a unique-id for each message, an arbitrary server-chosen string of one to 70 characters in the range 0x21 to 0x7E, which must persist across sessions. APOP, described earlier, is also optional.

RFC section 8 records an operational lesson. Clients found that using UIDL and never sending DELE gives a weak form of keeping mail on the server, as IMAP does. On large multi-user servers read mail then piles up without bound, so the RFC suggests per-user quotas or a retention policy, for example deleting unread messages after 60 days and read ones after 7. Such deletions are outside the protocol, and clients should still use DELE when appropriate.
sections.eli5: A few extra tricks: peek at the top of a letter without opening it, and give each letter a permanent label so you remember which ones you already took home.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section is brief and candid. It says it is only "conjectured" that APOP gives origin identification and replay protection. A server that supports both PASS and APOP should not allow both for the same mailbox name, and shared secrets should be long, since the example secret of eight characters is far too short.

It also lists plain facts. Servers that answer -ERR to USER tell attackers which names are valid. PASS sends the password in the clear, and RETR and TOP send mail in the clear. "Otherwise, security issues are not discussed in this memo."

This is a 1996 document. Later work addressed these gaps: RFC 2595 specifies using TLS with POP3, and RFC 8314 recommends TLS for mail access and calls cleartext obsolete. The MD5-based APOP design should not be treated as strong by modern standards.
sections.eli5: The first POP3 shouted passwords and letters across the room where anyone could hear. Later rules wrapped the whole conversation in a sealed tube.

items.title: DELE only marks
items.text: A deleted message disappears from listings but stays in the maildrop during the session.

items.title: QUIT commits
items.text: Only QUIT from the TRANSACTION state enters UPDATE and removes the marked messages.

items.title: Failure is safe
items.text: A dropped connection or autologout removes nothing.

items.title: Never extra
items.text: Even when removal fails, the server may not remove any message that was not marked.
